blocks.title: Unsaturated hydrocarbons
blocks.text: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons, unsaturated hydrocarbons are compounds of hydrogen and carbon only whose molecules contain carbon to carbon double bonds (or triple bonds).
Alkenes have two hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding saturated hydrocarbons.
The IUPAC rules for naming alkenes are similar in many respects to those for naming alkanes.
1. Select the longest continuous chain that contains the C = C as the parent chain. Change the ending of the name of the alkane of identical length from — ane to — ene, e.g.,
2. Number the chain so as to include both carbon atoms of the double bond. Numbering begins from the end nearer to the double bond.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the printed example carbon 5, which carries the CH₃ group, is written CH₂ and carbon 3 of the double bond is written C. Carbon 5 is CH and carbon 3 is CH: H₃C–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH=CH–CH₃ (5-methyl-2-hexene).
3. Designate the location of the double bond by using the number of the first atom of the double bond as a prefix.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed 1-butene and 1-pentene run into the text of rule 4: in 1-butene carbon 2 is printed CH₂ and carbon 3 is lost. The formulas are given above as they should read: 1-butene H₂C=CH–CH₂–CH₃ and 1-pentene H₂C=CH–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃.
4. Indicate the locations of the substituent groups by the numbers of the carbon atoms to which they are attached.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In both printed examples carbon 1 is written H₂C; it is H₃C. In 2,5,5-trimethyl-2-hexene carbon 4 is written CH₃; it is CH₂: H₃C–C(CH₃)=CH–CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–CH₃. 2-Methyl-2-butene is H₃C–C(CH₃)=CH–CH₃.
5. If the parent chain contains more than one double bonds, they are alkadienes for two, alkatrienes for three and so on.
